title: Convert a string to uppercase / lowercase without using built-in methods (add/subtract 32 from ASCII value).
shortTitle: Convert a String to Uppercase / Lowercase Without Built-in Methods

s1_definition.profdef: Converting letter case manually relies on the fact that in the ASCII table every lowercase letter sits exactly thirty-two positions above its uppercase counterpart. To uppercase, you subtract thirty-two from the code of any character in the lowercase a-to-z range; to lowercase, you add thirty-two to any character in the uppercase A-to-Z range. Characters outside those ranges are left untouched. You build the result in a StringBuilder in linear time because Java strings are immutable.
s1_definition.analogy: When the National Bank of India prints Rajesh's name on a statement, the formatting system must normalise it to a consistent case. Think of the alphabet as two parallel rows, big letters on top and small letters below, and the small row is exactly thirty-two steps to the right in the character numbering. To shout a letter in capitals we step it thirty-two places left; to make it small we step thirty-two places right. Anything that is not a letter, like a digit or a space in the name, we leave exactly as it is.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lowercase is thirty-two above uppercase in ASCII, so subtract thirty-two to capitalise and add thirty-two to make small, leaving non-letters alone.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Converting letter case manually relies on the fact that in the ASCII table every lowercase letter sits exactly thirty-two positions above its uppercase counterpart. To uppercase, you subtract thirty-two from the code of any character in the lowercase a-to-z range; to lowercase, you add thirty-two to any character in the uppercase A-to-Z range. Characters outside those ranges are left untouched. You build the result in a StringBuilder in linear time because Java strings are immutable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the National Bank of India prints Rajesh's name on a statement, the formatting system must normalise it to a consistent case. Think of the alphabet as two parallel rows, big letters on top and small letters below, and the small row is exactly thirty-two steps to the right in the character numbering. To shout a letter in capitals we step it thirty-two places left; to make it small we step thirty-two places right. Anything that is not a letter, like a digit or a space in the name, we leave exactly as it is.

**One line to remember:** Lowercase is thirty-two above uppercase in ASCII, so subtract thirty-two to capitalise and add thirty-two to make small, leaving non-letters alone.

sections.s2_technical:
In Java a char is really a number, its Unicode code point, and for the basic Latin letters that number matches the ASCII table. The uppercase A is sixty-five and the lowercase a is ninety-seven, a difference of exactly thirty-two, and the same gap holds for every letter pair through Z and z. That constant gap is what makes manual case conversion possible with simple arithmetic.

To uppercase a string, you loop over each character. If the character is in the lowercase range, meaning at least the character a and at most the character z, you subtract thirty-two to get the uppercase letter and append it; otherwise you append the character unchanged. To lowercase, you do the mirror image: if the character is in the uppercase range you add thirty-two, otherwise append unchanged.

A critical point is to only transform characters that are actually letters in the target range. If you blindly subtract thirty-two from every character you would corrupt digits, spaces, and punctuation. So the range check is not optional; it is what protects the non-letter characters in a name or code.

Because strings are immutable, you accumulate the converted characters in a StringBuilder and convert to a string at the end, which is linear in time and avoids creating a throwaway string on every character.

A senior point is the limit of this trick. It only works for the ASCII Latin letters A to Z and a to z. It does not correctly handle accented letters, other alphabets, or locale-specific rules such as the Turkish dotless i, where the real `toUpperCase` with a Locale behaves differently. So in production I use the built-in case methods with an explicit Locale for anything user-facing, and I reserve the manual thirty-two trick for controlled ASCII-only identifiers or for demonstrating that I understand the character encoding underneath. Being honest about this limitation is what separates a thoughtful answer from a naive one.

A small finance-domain example: `char c = 'a'; char upper = (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') ? (char)(c - 32) : c;` turns the lowercase a into uppercase A, while a digit like the character five would be left unchanged because it is outside the lowercase range.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, internal account codes like the one for Rajesh must be stored in a single canonical case so that lookups match regardless of how a clerk typed them. One clerk types the code in lowercase, another in uppercase, and the matching fails. The normalisation step forces every account code to uppercase. Converting case by the thirty-two rule is exactly this normalisation when the codes are guaranteed ASCII letters and digits.

This is exactly how manual case conversion works in Java — we step letters by thirty-two and leave digits untouched.

Problem 2 — The statement printer must also present Priya's display name in lowercase for a particular compact report style, but her name contains a space and may contain an accented character pasted from another system. This exposes the limit of the manual trick: it handles the plain letters and leaves the space alone, but it cannot correctly lowercase an accented letter, which is why the code logs a warning and why for real user-facing names the built-in locale-aware method is the right tool.

What the code will do: a `CaseConverter` class with `toUpperAscii(String s)` and `toLowerAscii(String s)` implementing the thirty-two rule with range checks. The demo normalises Rajesh's account code to uppercase and lowercases a display string, showing that non-letters are preserved.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's code is `sav2001` and Priya's name is `Priya SHARMA`.

Step 1: `toUpperAscii("sav2001")` runs. We create a StringBuilder pre-sized to `7`.

Step 2: We loop. The character `s` is in the lowercase range, so we subtract thirty-two, giving `S`, and append it. Likewise `a` becomes `A` and `v` becomes `V`, so far `SAV`.

Step 3: The next characters are `2`, `0`, `0`, `1`. These are digits, outside the lowercase range, so the range check fails and we append each unchanged. The result is `SAV2001`. The digits were protected by the range check.

Step 4: `toLowerAscii("Priya SHARMA")` runs. The character `P` is in the uppercase range, so we add thirty-two, giving `p`. The characters `r`, `i`, `y`, `a` are already lowercase and outside the uppercase range, so they are appended unchanged, giving `priya`.

Step 5: The next character is a space. It is not in the uppercase range and is within ASCII, so it is appended unchanged, preserving the gap between first and last name.

Step 6: The remaining characters `S`, `H`, `A`, `R`, `M`, `A` are each in the uppercase range, so each gets thirty-two added, giving `sharma`. The final string is `priya sharma`. No input was mutated; each conversion built a fresh string.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:10:00Z INFO Rajesh code normalised to upper: 'SAV2001'
2026-10-26T15:10:00Z INFO Priya name to lower: 'priya sharma'
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "sav2001" and "Priya SHARMA"
    │
    ▼
  toUpperAscii("sav2001")
    │ s,a,v in [a..z] → -32 → S,A,V
    │ 2,0,0,1 outside range → unchanged
    ▼
  "SAV2001"
    │
    ▼
  toLowerAscii("Priya SHARMA")
    │ P in [A..Z] → +32 → p ; riya unchanged
    │ ' ' preserved ; SHARMA → +32 each → sharma
    ▼
  "priya sharma"
    │
    ▼
  Output: canonical-case identifiers (non-letters preserved)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Manual case conversion relies on the ASCII layout: every lowercase letter is exactly thirty-two above its uppercase counterpart, because uppercase A is sixty-five and lowercase a is ninety-seven. So to uppercase I subtract thirty-two from any character in the lowercase a-to-z range, and to lowercase I add thirty-two to any character in the uppercase A-to-Z range, building the result in a StringBuilder because strings are immutable.

The non-negotiable part is the range check. I only transform characters that are actually letters in the target range and append everything else unchanged, otherwise I would corrupt digits, spaces, and punctuation. In a name or an account code that range check is what protects the non-letter characters.

I am always honest about the limitation of this trick in an interview. It works only for the basic ASCII Latin letters. It does not handle accented characters, other alphabets, or locale-specific rules like the Turkish dotless i, where the real toUpperCase with an explicit Locale behaves differently. So for anything user-facing I use the built-in case methods with a Locale, and I keep the manual thirty-two trick for controlled ASCII-only identifiers or to show I understand the encoding underneath.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used it to normalise internal account codes to a single canonical uppercase so lookups match no matter how a clerk typed them, with the digits in the code left untouched by the range check. For display names I deliberately fall back to the locale-aware method and log a warning when a non-ASCII character appears, because getting a customer's name wrong on a statement is not acceptable. Explaining both the trick and its limits shows the interviewer I understand character encoding and know when the clever shortcut is the wrong choice.
